newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Siemens sees lower near term chip profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Siemens sees lower near term chip profit.

text.p: The semiconductor unit of German giant Siemens AG, while predicting dramatic long-term sales growth, said on Thursday it expected soft chip prices to pressure profit over the next two years.

Pretax profit this year would fall short of the 603 milion marks ($357 million) reported for 1995/96, Siemens semiconductor (HL) said. Profit was likely to halt its fall in 1997/98 but probably would not top the 1995/96 level.

"Naturally we have a challenge this year," said HL sales chief Peter Fischl at a news conference. "It all depends on the price dynamic. We have work to do but we are optimistic we will be in the black for this year."
Over the past 18 months, chip prices have fallen as much as 80 percent on some commodity memory chips called DRAMs.
Fischl declined to comment on analyst forecasts that HL pretax profit would fall by about two thirds to around 200 million marks this year.

At the same time, rising costs would also pressure profit in the near term, he said. In 1995/96, which ended September 30, capital investment climbed 71 percent to 2.2 billion marks, while the payroll rose 22 percent to 19,316 workers.
Longer term, HL predicted overseas expansion and strategic manufacturing partnerships to nearly triple sales to around 14 billion marks by 2001, although soft chip prices would dampen 1996/97 profit.

Siemens semiconductors (HL) forecast 26 percent annual sales growth over the next five years -- compared to a rate of 15 percent for the chip market as a whole during that time, HL chief executive Ulrich Schumacher said.
"Siemens is banking on the semiconductor market reviving in the medium term," he said. "We have set a target of nearly trebling sales by 2001."
Peter Roe, a Siemens analysts at Banque Paribas Capital Markets in London, said HL's goal of tripling sales was "challenging but not unrealistic."

"HL is exposed to some commodity prices but it has modern (manufacturing) capacity and is well placed in other segments where growth will be strong," he said. "HL is a powerful long-term engine but isn't firing on all cylinders right now."

Schumacher said most of the growth would come in Asia and the United States, where Siemens, the world's 12th-largest chip maker, expected annual semiconductor market growth of 15 percent and 16 percent respectively between now and 2001.
To support international growth Siemens planned to expand manufacturing capacity outside Germany and link up with other chip companies, he said.

"A worldwide presence, with manufacturing capacity on site and the move away from exports is only one step to making the semiconductor group a global player," he said. "Strategic alliances with other global players play a decisive role."
The company has already started chip plants with Motorola Inc. in the U.S. and with Mosel Vitelic in Taiwan.
Siemens forecast chip market growth of six percent in 1997, accelerating to 18 percent in 1998, and 22 percent in 1999.
Chip pricing should stabilise next year as the Internet, expanding corporate networks, increasing use of mobile phones and wireless communications drive demand for semiconductors.
Falling prices caused HL net income to fall 24 percent to 603 million marks in 1995/96. Its pretax profits of 603 million marks made it Siemens' most profitable unit last year.

Sales last year grew only one percent in Germany and in the rest of Europe, to 1.7 billion marks and 1.2 billion marks respectively. North American sales rose 38 percent to 775 million marks and Asian sales gained 23 percent to 871 million.
In the three-month period that ended December, HL sales were down 12 percent at one billion marks. First quarter orders were down 24 percent at 1.2 billion marks.
HL's profit outlook was one of the main reasons Siemens forecast no improvement in overall group earnings for 1996/97.
($ = 1.687 German Marks)
